_about: Per-pest seasonal activity, each a VERBATIM quote from a named public source with a working URL, paired with that city's own retrieved NOAA figures. Same rule as mold-materials: no source, no entry. A pest with no citable statement gets NO block at all — a freeze window on a bed bug page would be filler, and bed bugs have no season.
_why_both_halves: The quote alone is national and adds nothing Google cannot get from CDC or the extension service directly. The local figures alone are climate, not pest. It is the pairing that is new: published biology set against this city's own measured climate, both cited. That is the information gain.

_not_included.others: ant, carpenter ant, flea, wasp, bee, spider, cricket, silverfish, rodent — not yet attempted. Adding one is a JSON entry, no code.

fire-ant-control.heading: When are fire ants active in {city}, {SS}?
fire-ant-control.verbatim: Foraging activity slows when soil temperature is lower than 65 to 70 °F or higher than 90 °F.
also: Mating flights are most common in spring and fall.
fire-ant-control.context: Because that is a temperature rule rather than a date, it can be read directly against the local figures below — the months that cross 90 °F are the months when foraging slows at the top end.

stink-bug-control.heading: When do stink bugs come indoors in {city}, {SS}?
stink-bug-control.verbatim: Adults begin to search for overwintering sites starting in September through October.
also: Adults emerge in the spring (late April to mid-May)
stink-bug-control.context: Two windows rather than one, then: into the building through autumn, back out the following spring.

termite-treatment.label: termite
termite-treatment.heading: When do termites swarm in {city}, {SS}?
termite-treatment.verbatim: Native subterranean termites begin swarming in February/March, swarm during the day, and are not attracted to lights.

also.verbatim: Formosan termites (1) swarm at night; (2) swarm in late May and/or early June (in Georgia), and (3) swarmers are attracted to light.
In Pennsylvania, swarms of winged termites usually emerge between February and June.

termite-treatment.context: The behavior is the part that travels: a swarm in daylight that ignores a porch light is a native subterranean termite, while a swarm after dark drawn to the light is Formosan. The months do not travel — the same native species begins in February or March in Georgia but can emerge any time from February to June in Pennsylvania, so the dates below matter more than either range.
termite-treatment.local: In {city} the average last spring freeze falls on {freeze_last_spring}, and the frost-free stretch runs to {freeze_first_fall} — about {frost_free_days} days.

mosquito-control.verbatim: These insects are most active when the temperatures are above 50°F, meaning they're here in the South for a good chunk of the year.
mosquito-control.context: The 50°F line is the transferable part, and because it is a temperature rather than a date it can be read against the figures below instead of against a calendar written for somewhere else. The second half of that sentence is Mississippi-specific, which is precisely why the local numbers belong next to it.

intros: Two things decide when you see a pest: what the species does, and what the weather here actually does. Below is the published guidance on the first, set against this city's own measured climate.
Seasonal advice is usually written for the whole country. These are the published figures for the species, placed next to the measured climate for this city specifically.
What follows is the published seasonal guidance for this pest, and the recorded climate normals for this city, so the two can be read together rather than one standing in for the other.

_sourcing_notes.tick-treatment: CDC's sentence carries its own year-round caveat, so it is quoted whole. Trimming it to 'April-September' would make it say something CDC deliberately does not say.
_sourcing_notes.fire-ant-control: The strongest entry in this file, because it is a temperature threshold rather than a calendar and therefore pairs directly with the city's own measured temperatures instead of restating a generic season.
_sourcing_notes.stink-bug-control: Two separate quotes from one source, giving both ends of the cycle. Both sit either side of this city's own freeze dates, which is what makes the local figures worth printing beside them.
_sourcing_notes.termite-treatment: No species-to-region map was obtainable from a source passing our own test: UGA C868 is Georgia-specific on distribution and LSU AgCenter, the actual authority, serves an unverifiable certificate. So the entry leads with the day/night and light-attraction contrast, which is geography-independent and more actionable than a month range, and quotes BOTH a Georgia and a Pennsylvania window — each against its own source — to show the months are regional rather than implying one applies everywhere.
_sourcing_notes.mosquito-control: Third attempt. CDC's current pages carry no temperature threshold and the ubiquitous 'below 50F they go dormant' traces only to a 1970s CDC handbook PDF; two rounds of extension searches returned academic papers and patents. MSU Extension states it in HTML, so that is the citation, quoted whole including 'here in the South'.
_sourcing_notes.termite-inspection: alias_of termite-treatment. Both inspection pages are about finding termites, so the swarm-behavior cues apply unchanged; only the heading differs.

_per_city: `local` may be a list of {when, text} variants tested against the city's own retrieved figures. The quote is identical fleet-wide by necessity; the sentence around it is not. This is variation because the data differs, not variation for its own sake.
_why_no_needs_key: A `needs` list was declared on several entries and never read — the mold-materials audit finding repeated. pest_season_local() already enforces it: a sentence whose token will not resolve is voided entirely rather than rendered with a gap, so the requirement is expressed by the code that depends on it.
